claim: The Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) is one of the most abundant mammals with a nearly worldwide distribution.
source: The Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus, hereafter referred to as rat) is one of the most abundant mammals with a nearly worldwide distribution (Galef, 2009; Puckett et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galef, 2009 and Puckett et al., 2016.

claim: Almost all wild rats live in close association with humans.
source: Today, almost all wild rats live in close association with humans, leading to various forms of adverse interactions (Barnett, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 2001.

claim: Rats are known to transmit diseases.
source: For example, rats are known to transmit diseases (Himsworth et al., 2013b), destroy stored food (Meerburg et al., 2009) and damage infrastructure by gnawing on wires or fundaments (Booy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Himsworth et al., 2013b.

claim: Rats destroy stored food.
source: For example, rats are known to transmit diseases (Himsworth et al., 2013b), destroy stored food (Meerburg et al., 2009) and damage infrastructure by gnawing on wires or fundaments (Booy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meerburg et al., 2009.

claim: Rats damage infrastructure by gnawing on wires or fundaments.
source: For example, rats are known to transmit diseases (Himsworth et al., 2013b), destroy stored food (Meerburg et al., 2009) and damage infrastructure by gnawing on wires or fundaments (Booy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Booy et al., 2017.

claim: Rats cost the US economy a minimum of two billion dollars each year.
source: Consequently, it has been estimated that rats cost only the US economy a minimum of two billion dollars each year (Pimentel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pimentel et al., 2005.

claim: Rats are predators that can be a threat to other species, especially when introduced to a new area.
source: Furthermore, rats are predators that can be a threat to other species, especially when introduced to a new area (Moors et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moors et al., 1992.

claim: In 2030 it is expected that more than 75% of all humans will live in cities.
source: Today, controlling rat populations is becoming ever more important since the human population grows with increasing speed and in 2030 it is expected that more than 75% of all humans will live in cities, which means that they most likely will live together with rats (Cohen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen, 2003.

claim: Rat population control remains ineffective.
source: Therefore, interactions with rats are likely to increase in the future, if the rat population control remains that ineffective (Parsons et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parsons et al., 2017.

claim: Approximately 100,000 pet rats lived in the UK in 2019.
source: Whereas wild rats are undesired in close proximity to humans, domesticated rats are more than welcome as pet rats in households, where approximately 100'000 lived in 2019 in the UK alone (PFMA, 2020), and as laboratory rats in scientific institutes, where more than 20 million rats are used worldwide for research every year (Baumans, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to PFMA, 2020.

claim: More than 20 million rats are used worldwide for research every year.
source: Whereas wild rats are undesired in close proximity to humans, domesticated rats are more than welcome as pet rats in households, where approximately 100'000 lived in 2019 in the UK alone (PFMA, 2020), and as laboratory rats in scientific institutes, where more than 20 million rats are used worldwide for research every year (Baumans, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baumans, 2004.

claim: The first described scientific experiment using rats as model organism dates back to the 1850s.
source: The first described scientific experiment using rats as model organism dates back to the 1850s (Philipeaux, 1856).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Philipeaux, 1856.

claim: Over 350 different laboratory rat strains are available today.
source: Ever since, rats turned into one of the most important model organisms, resulting in over 350 different laboratory strains available today (http://www.rrrc.us/search/).
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to a website (http://www.rrrc.us/search/).

claim: In 2004, the full genome of one rat strain (BN/SsNHsd) was sequenced.
source: In 2004, the full genome of one strain (BN/SsNHsd) was sequenced, which further increased the possibilities of research in the fields of biochemistry, genetics, genomics and physiology (Gibbs et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gibbs et al., 2004.

claim: Worldwide approximately one study is published per hour that used rats as model organism.
source: Today, it has been estimated that worldwide approximately one study is published per hour that used rats as model organism (Berdoy, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berdoy, 2002.

claim: Poor welfare can impact the quality of science and may be one factor of the reproducibility crisis in science.
source: Moreover, it has been pointed out that poor welfare can impact the quality of science and may hence be one factor of the reproducibility crisis in science (Garner, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garner, 2005.

claim: There is a general assumption that wild rats are not being particularly prosocial towards their conspecifics.
source: Despite these challenges, there is the general assumption that wild rats are not being particularly prosocial towards their conspecifics (e.g., Barnett, 1957; Feng and Himsworth, 2014; Inglis et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett, 1957; Feng and Himsworth, 2014; Inglis et al., 1996.

claim: Recent laboratory studies show that rats are highly social animals that depend strongly on conspecific cooperative interactions.
source: This stands in stark contrast to recent laboratory studies showing that rats are highly social animals that depend strongly on conspecific cooperative interactions and consequently show elaborate prosocial behaviours, such as freeing trapped partners and exchanging favours (Mogil, 2019; Schweinfurth, 2020; Wrighten and Hall, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mogil, 2019; Schweinfurth, 2020; Wrighten and Hall, 2016.

claim: Domestication of rats started in the 19th century.
source: Since domestication of rats has started in the 19th century (Lindsey and Baker, 2006), it is sensible to assume that selective breeding and adaptions in response to artificial environments occurred and hence wild rats differ from domesticated rats in their social behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lindsey and Baker, 2006.

claim: Wild rats have the propensity to rapidly adapt to environmental changes.
source: Furthermore, wild rats have the propensity to rapidly adapt to environmental changes (Johnson and Munshi-South, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson and Munshi-South, 2017.

claim: Wild rats burrow less than domesticated rats.
source: In accordance, direct comparisons between the behaviour of wild and domesticated rats show that, for instance, wild rats burrow less (Price, 1973), are more neophobic (Mitchell, 1976), learn more slowly (Boice, 1972) and are more aggressive towards conspecifics (de Boer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Price, 1973.

claim: Wild rats are more neophobic than domesticated rats.
source: In accordance, direct comparisons between the behaviour of wild and domesticated rats show that, for instance, wild rats burrow less (Price, 1973), are more neophobic (Mitchell, 1976), learn more slowly (Boice, 1972) and are more aggressive towards conspecifics (de Boer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mitchell, 1976.

claim: Wild rats learn more slowly than domesticated rats.
source: In accordance, direct comparisons between the behaviour of wild and domesticated rats show that, for instance, wild rats burrow less (Price, 1973), are more neophobic (Mitchell, 1976), learn more slowly (Boice, 1972) and are more aggressive towards conspecifics (de Boer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boice, 1972.

claim: Wild rats are more aggressive towards conspecifics than domesticated rats.
source: In accordance, direct comparisons between the behaviour of wild and domesticated rats show that, for instance, wild rats burrow less (Price, 1973), are more neophobic (Mitchell, 1976), learn more slowly (Boice, 1972) and are more aggressive towards conspecifics (de Boer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Boer et al., 2003.

claim: Wild rats dominate domesticated rats in direct interactions.
source: Consequently, wild rats dominate domesticated rats in direct interactions (Boreman and Price, 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boreman and Price, 1972.

claim: The differences between wild and domesticated rats are rather quantitative than qualitative.
source: However, the described differences between wild and domesticated rats are rather quantitative than qualitative (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: Domesticated rats show the full behavioural repertoire of wild rats.
source: Indeed, domesticated rats show the full behavioural repertoire of wild rats (Boice, 1981; Boice, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boice, 1981 and Boice, 1973.

claim: Domesticated rats have been shown to survive and reproduce under semi-natural conditions.
source: Consequently, domesticated rats have been shown to survive and reproduce under semi-natural conditions (Adams and Boice, 1983; Blanchard et al., 1988; Boice, 1977), even if predators were present (Berdoy, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adams and Boice, 1983; Blanchard et al., 1988; Boice, 1977; Berdoy, 2002.

claim: Wild rats live almost exclusively in close contact with humans.
source: Wild rats live almost exclusively in close contact with humans (Singleton et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Singleton et al., 2003.

claim: Wild rats live in large colonies, which may be composed of more than 150 individuals.
source: Wild rats live in large colonies, which, dependent upon food resources, may be composed of more than 150 individuals (Davis, 1953).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis, 1953.

claim: Rat colonies are usually structured into subgroups.
source: Colonies are usually structured into subgroups, which might consist of pairs, harems with or without offspring, unisexual groups and/or single males and females (Calhoun, 1979; de Boer et al., 2016; Timmermans, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Calhoun, 1979; de Boer et al., 2016; Timmermans, 1978.

claim: Wild rats jointly excavate a burrow system, which consists of tunnels and chambers that serve as shared nest sites as well as places for food storage.
source: Wild rats jointly excavate a burrow system, which consists of tunnels and chambers that serve as shared nest sites as well as places for food storage (Telle, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Telle, 1966.

claim: Outside their burrow, rats establish a trail system, which is marked by olfactory cues and serve as foraging paths as well as connections between sites.
source: Outside their burrow, rats establish a trail system, which is marked by olfactory cues and serve as foraging paths as well as connections between sites (Telle, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Telle, 1966.

claim: Mothers form strong bonds with their infants until these are around two months old.
source: Studies on wild rats under semi-natural conditions showed that while mothers form strong bonds with their infants until these are around two months old, there is no evidence that adult wild rats form stable pair bonds (e.g., Barnett, 1963; Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett, 1963 and Calhoun, 1979.

claim: There is no evidence that adult wild rats form stable pair bonds.
source: Studies on wild rats under semi-natural conditions showed that while mothers form strong bonds with their infants until these are around two months old, there is no evidence that adult wild rats form stable pair bonds (e.g., Barnett, 1963; Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett, 1963 and Calhoun, 1979.

claim: Wild-derived females do not form selective social bonds in captivity.
source: In line with this, wild-derived females also do not form selective social bonds in captivity (Schweinfurth et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schweinfurth et al., 2017a.

claim: Female rats form rather loose hierarchies under captive and semi-natural conditions.
source: Probably based on their oestrus cycle, female rats form rather loose hierarchies under captive (domesticated and wild rats: Ziporyn and McClintock, 1991; wild-derived: Schweinfurth et al., 2017a) and semi-natural conditions (Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ziporyn and McClintock, 1991; Schweinfurth et al., 2017a; Calhoun, 1979.

claim: Under semi-natural conditions, males form more pronounced, stable and near-linear hierarchies based on fighting abilities.
source: Under the latter conditions, males form more pronounced, stable and near-linear hierarchies based on fighting abilities (Berdoy et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berdoy et al., 1995.

claim: Three main male types have been identified: Alpha males, Beta males, and Omega males.
source: Three main male types have been identified (Barnett, 1963): Alpha males are the largest individuals in the colony, move freely and initiate attacks on intruders. Beta males shy away from alpha males but can gain weight. Lowest ranking omega males generally lose weight and do not reproduce.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: Omega males often disperse from their natal colony.
source: Therefore, omega males often disperse from their natal colony.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statement that omega males lose weight and do not reproduce.

claim: Overt aggression between colony members occurs infrequently in wild rats under semi-natural conditions.
source: Studies on wild rats under semi-natural conditions showed that overt aggression between colony members occurs infrequently (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: Most agonistic behaviours in rats are directed against intruders from outside the colony.
source: Instead, most agonistic behaviours are directed against intruders from outside the colony (Blanchard et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blanchard et al., 1988.

claim: Males seem to be less socially tolerant than females.
source: In general, males seem to be less socially tolerant than females (Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun, 1979.

claim: Solely males patrol and defend the territory borders.
source: Hence, solely males patrol and defend the territory boarders.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statement that males are less socially tolerant than females.

claim: Females defend their breeding chamber when lactating.
source: Females, in contrast, seem to be less territorial, but defend their breeding chamber when lactating (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: Domesticated rats are known to kill conspecifics under limited space conditions in the laboratory.
source: Although domesticated rats are known to kill conspecifics under limited space conditions in the laboratory (e.g., Blanchard et al., 1975), there is no evidence that rats kill each other under natural conditions, in which there is enough space for separation (Barnett, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blanchard et al., 1975 and Barnett, 2001.

claim: There is no evidence that rats kill each other under natural conditions, in which there is enough space for separation.
source: Although domesticated rats are known to kill conspecifics under limited space conditions in the laboratory (e.g., Blanchard et al., 1975), there is no evidence that rats kill each other under natural conditions, in which there is enough space for separation (Barnett, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 2001.

claim: Domesticated rats show lower levels of aggression compared to wild rats.
source: Although domesticated rats show lower levels of aggression compared to wild rats, they show the same repertoire of aggressive behaviours (Plyusnina et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Plyusnina et al., 2011.

claim: Domesticated rats show the same repertoire of aggressive behaviours as wild rats.
source: Although domesticated rats show lower levels of aggression compared to wild rats, they show the same repertoire of aggressive behaviours (Plyusnina et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Plyusnina et al., 2011.

claim: A frequent affiliative behaviour in wild rats is allogrooming, where one individual licks or nibbles the fur of a conspecific.
source: A frequent affiliative behaviour in wild rats is allogrooming, where one individual licks or nibbles the fur of a conspecific (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: In wild-derived female rats, allogrooming is directed preferably to spots that are difficult to reach for the groomed individual, such as the face or neck.
source: In wild-derived female rats such allogrooming is directed preferably to spots that are difficult to reach for the groomed individual, such as the face or neck (Schweinfurth et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schweinfurth et al., 2017b.

claim: Wild rats experience allogrooming early in life, as it is directed from mothers towards infants.
source: Wild rats experience such grooming already early in life, as it is directed from mothers towards infants. Later, infants transfer this behaviour to other colony members (Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun, 1979.

claim: As wild rats share the same feeding sites, some colony members share food with others either by allowing them to take food or by letting them lick off residues from their fur.
source: As wild rats share the same feeding sites, some colony members share food with others either by allowing them to take food (Barnett, 1963; Galef et al., 2001) or by letting them lick off residues from their fur (Barnett, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett, 1963; Galef et al., 2001; Barnett, 1956.

claim: Huddling is common amongst altricial infants and is beneficial for thermoregulation.
source: Huddling, where rats lie together piled in a heap on top of each other, is beneficial for thermoregulation and thus, common amongst altricial infants (domesticated rats: Alberts, 2006; Sokoloff and Blumberg, 2001; wild rats: Calhoun, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alberts, 2006; Sokoloff and Blumberg, 2001; Calhoun, 1979.

claim: Adult rats huddle together, even under warm conditions and when there is ample opportunity to separate.
source: Moreover, adult rats huddle together, even under warm conditions and when there is ample opportunity to separate, which suggests some social function beyond thermoregulation.
evidence: The claim is based on observation and inference about social function.

claim: When pioneering, one rat vigilantly leaves the burrow and observes the surroundings for several minutes, and only then will other colony members appear from the burrow.
source: When pioneering, one rat vigilantly leaves the burrow and observes the surroundings for several minutes. Only then will other colony members appear from the burrow as well (Barnett and Spencer, 1951; Telle, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett and Spencer, 1951 and Telle, 1966.

claim: Wild rats have been reported to play with each other.
source: Although wild rats have been reported to play with each other (Calhoun, 1979, p.180; Ewer, 1971), most evidence of social play is based on work on domesticated rats (reviewed in: Himmler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Calhoun, 1979 and Ewer, 1971.

claim: Domesticated rats engage in play fights, so-called rough-and-tumble play, when they are about 17 days old and retain this behaviour until they reach sexual maturity.
source: Domesticated rats engage in play fights, so-called rough-and-tumble play, when they are about 17 days old and retain this behaviour until they reach sexual maturity (Thor and Holloway, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thor and Holloway, 1984.

claim: During play fights, young domesticated and wild-derived rats wrestle, box and kick each other in order to turn the opponent on the back and attack the nape.
source: During play fights, young domesticated and wild-derived rats wrestle, box and kick each other in order to turn the opponent on the back and attack the nape (Himmler et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Himmler et al., 2013.

claim: Wild-derived rats show less social play compared to domesticated rats and their play involves less body contact.
source: The same study found that wild-derived rats show less social play compared to domesticated rats and their play involves less body contact.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to the same study (Himmler et al., 2013).

claim: Domesticated rats emit 50 kHz calls during social play.
source: Domesticated rats emit 50 kHz calls during such play (Burgdorf et al., 2008), which are associated with positive emotions (Burgdorf and Panksepp, 2001) and hence point towards rewarding effects of social play.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgdorf et al., 2008 and Burgdorf and Panksepp, 2001.

claim: Wild rats reach sexual maturity at an age of two to three months.
source: Wild rats reach sexual maturity at an age of two to three months (Clark and Price, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clark and Price, 1981.

claim: Both sexes of wild rats are highly promiscuous.
source: Both sexes are highly promiscuous, and males are usually not able to monopolise single females due to the presence of many other males in the colony (MacDonald et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to MacDonald et al., 1999.

claim: Wild females have a short oestrus cycle of one to two weeks.
source: Furthermore, compared to other mammals, wild females have a short oestrus cycle of one to two weeks (McClintock and Adler, 1978), which is further reduced to only four days in domesticated rats (Marcondes et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McClintock and Adler, 1978 and Marcondes et al., 2002.

claim: Domesticated males have been selected for increased fecundity and thus show enlarged testes and reach maturity earlier than wild rats.
source: Like other domesticated animals, domesticated males have been selected for increased fecundity and thus show also enlarged testes and reach maturity earlier than wild rats (Clark and Price, 1981; Setchell, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark and Price, 1981 and Setchell, 1992.

claim: When living in large groups, several males follow the receptive female during their short receptive period before copulation.
source: When living in large groups, several males follow the receptive female during their short receptive period before copulation (Berdoy et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berdoy et al., 1995.

claim: Most of the males successfully copulate with the female repeatedly.
source: Most of the males successfully copulate with the female repeatedly (MacDonald et al., 1999; Steininger, 1950).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 1999 and Steininger, 1950.

claim: After ejaculation, domesticated male rats in the laboratory insert a vaginal plug, which dissolves after 12 hr.
source: After ejaculation, domesticated male rats in the laboratory insert a vaginal plug, which dissolves after 12 hr (Austin and Dewsbury, 1986), but so far there is no evidence for these plugs in wild rats.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Austin and Dewsbury, 1986.

claim: There is no evidence for vaginal plugs in wild rats.
source: After ejaculation, domesticated male rats in the laboratory insert a vaginal plug, which dissolves after 12 hr (Austin and Dewsbury, 1986), but so far there is no evidence for these plugs in wild rats.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of evidence.

claim: Pregnant laboratory females resorb their embryos, if they smell cat urine in their nest during the first third of gestation.
source: For instance, pregnant laboratory females resorb their embryos, if they smell cat urine in their nest during the first third of gestation (Voznessenskaya et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Voznessenskaya et al., 2002.

claim: Mathematical models showed that fertility control methods can be as effective as more traditional methods, such as baiting and trapping.
source: Importantly, mathematical models showed that such fertility control methods can be as effective as more traditional methods, such as baiting and trapping (Zhang, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang, 2000.

claim: Approximately three weeks after copulation, females give birth to a litter of four to eight pups in wild rats and eight to sixteen pups in domesticated rats.
source: Approximately three weeks after copulation, females give birth to a litter of four to eight pups in wild rats and eight to sixteen pups in domesticated rats (Calhoun, 1979; Clark and Price, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Calhoun, 1979 and Clark and Price, 1981.

claim: Domesticated rats breed communally under laboratory conditions.
source: Whereas domesticated rats breed communally under laboratory conditions (e.g., Mennella et al., 2014), this has not been confirmed under natural conditions (Barnett, 1963; Calhoun, 1979; Telle, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mennella et al., 2014; Barnett, 1963; Calhoun, 1979; Telle, 1966.

claim: In wild rats, pups are born in a private underground chamber of the communal burrow.
source: Here, pups are born in a private underground chamber of the communal burrow (Davis, 1953).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis, 1953.

claim: Males show no paternal care.
source: Males show no paternal care, whereas females nurse the altricial offspring until weaning at approximately 40 days (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: Females nurse the altricial offspring until weaning at approximately 40 days.
source: Males show no paternal care, whereas females nurse the altricial offspring until weaning at approximately 40 days (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett, 1963.

claim: After weaning, the offspring stays in close association with their mother for up to two months.
source: Thereafter, the offspring stays in close association with their mother for up to two months (Calhoun, 1979), which stands in contrast to the common practice of breeders to separate offspring from their mother at the age of three weeks.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun, 1979.

claim: Offspring of highly attentive mothers show low plasma corticosterone levels, modest stress responses, better spatial learning, increased memory and become attentive mothers later in life.
source: For instance, offspring of highly attentive mothers, which intensively lick and groom their offspring, show low plasma corticosterone levels, modest stress responses, better spatial learning, increased memory and become attentive mothers later in life, too.
evidence: The claim is based on research reviewed in Champagne, 2008; Champagne and Curley, 2009; Liu et al., 2000; Weaver et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Groups of wild rats are socially complex as they live in long-term groups of multiple generations, which allows for repeated interactions with differently familiar and related individuals.
source: Groups of wild rats are socially complex as they live in long-term groups of multiple generations, which allows for repeated interactions with differently familiar and related individuals (see Scheiber et al., 2017 for the characteristics of social complexity).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scheiber et al., 2017.

claim: Rats distinguish not only between kin and non-kin, but also between different degrees of relatedness on the level of cousins.
source: Indeed, rats distinguish not only between kin and non-kin (domesticated rats: Hepper, 1987a; Zhang and Zhang, 2011; wild-derived rats: Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018a), but also between different degrees of relatedness on the level of cousins (domesticated rats: Hepper, 1987b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hepper, 1987a; Zhang and Zhang, 2011; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018a; Hepper, 1987b.

claim: This ability is probably the result of prenatal imprinting, as rat pups prefer the amniotic fluid of their mother, even if they were born by Caesarean section.
source: This ability is probably the result of prenatal imprinting, as rat pups prefer the amniotic fluid of their mother, even if they were born by Caesarean section (Hepper, 1987a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hepper, 1987a.

claim: Wild rats are able to discriminate colony members from intruders.
source: In addition, wild rats are able to discriminate colony members from intruders (Alberts and Galef, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alberts and Galef, 1973.

claim: Domesticated rats can truly differentiate between single conspecifics based on individually distinct odour cues after they were given the opportunity to learn such cues.
source: Remarkably, domesticated rats can truly differentiate between single conspecifics based on individually distinct odour cues after they were given the opportunity to learn such cues, instead of just using familiarity based heuristics (Gheusi et al., 1997; Hopp et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gheusi et al., 1997 and Hopp et al., 1985.

claim: Domesticated rats are capable of assessing the emotional state of other individuals.
source: Besides being able to identify others, domesticated rats are also capable of assessing the emotional state of other individuals, allowing them to predict future behaviour.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the text.

claim: Rats show a large repertoire of facial expressions.
source: Rats show a large repertoire of facial expressions (Sotocinal et al., 2015), which are used to evaluate emotional states of conspecifics (Nakashima et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sotocinal et al., 2015 and Nakashima et al., 2015.

claim: Rats collect information of emotional states by odour cues from urine, which signal if another individual is stressed or frustrated.
source: Furthermore, they collect information of emotional states by odour cues from urine, which signal if another individual is stressed (Valenta and Rigby, 1968) or frustrated (Morrison and Ludvigson, 1970).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Valenta and Rigby, 1968 and Morrison and Ludvigson, 1970.

claim: There is ample evidence that rats are capable of showing emotional contagion.
source: There is ample evidence that rats are capable of showing emotional contagion.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple studies cited in the text.

claim: When familiar with a particular stressor, domesticated rats stop moving, if realising that other individuals are experiencing this stressor.
source: When familiar with a particular stressor, domesticated rats stop moving, if realising that other individuals are experiencing this stressor (Atsak et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Atsak et al., 2011.

claim: If rats previously experienced electro-shocks for certain actions themselves, they stop pressing a self-rewarding lever, if they observe a partner being electro-shocked for their action.
source: Furthermore, if rats previously experienced electro-shocks for certain actions themselves, they stop pressing a self-rewarding lever, if they observe a partner being electro-shocked for their action (Church, 1959).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Church, 1959.

claim: Rats learn to avoid situations that are harmful to others, even if they never experienced the harmful situation themselves.
source: Finally, rats learn to avoid situations that are harmful to others, even if they never experienced the harmful situation themselves (e.g., Knapska et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knapska et al., 2010.

claim: The smell of a stressed conspecific's urine can elicit a stress response in rats.
source: Thereby it is not necessary for them to observe the behaviour of other rats because the smell of a stressed conspecific's urine can elicit a stress response (Mackay-Sim and Laing, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mackay-Sim and Laing, 1981.

claim: Rats have a high motivation to help each other, exemplified by their preference to cooperate, even if it is possible to achieve the same reward individually.
source: Rats have a high motivation to help each other, exemplified by their preference to cooperate, even if it is possible to achieve the same reward individually (Schuster and Perelberg, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schuster and Perelberg, 2004.

claim: Domesticated rats can coordinate their behaviour with conspecifics to avoid electric shocks or to gain rewards for themselves and their partner.
source: For instance, domesticated rats can coordinate their behaviour with conspecifics to avoid electric shocks (Daniel, 1942) or to gain rewards for themselves and their partner (Schuster, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daniel, 1942 and Schuster, 2002.

claim: Such coordination for a mutual benefit is independent of sex, strain or familiarity between the test animals.
source: Such coordination for a mutual benefit is independent of sex (Schuster et al., 1993), strain (Schuster et al., 1988) or familiarity (Tan and Hackenberg, 2016) between the test animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schuster et al., 1993; Schuster et al., 1988; Tan and Hackenberg, 2016.

claim: Rats housed in isolation are not able to coordinate their behaviour with conspecifics.
source: However, rats housed in isolation are not able to coordinate their behaviour with conspecifics (Swanson and Schuster, 1987), suggesting the social environment being necessary in developing social skills.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swanson and Schuster, 1987.

claim: When given the choice between delivering a reward to either themselves only or also to a partner at no cost, domesticated rats opt for the latter mutually-rewarding option.
source: When given the choice between delivering a reward to either themselves only or also to a partner at no cost, domesticated rats opt for the latter mutually-rewarding option (Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2016; Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2014; Márquez et al., 2015; Oberliessen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2016; Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2014; Márquez et al., 2015; Oberliessen et al., 2016.

claim: Domesticated and wild rats have been shown to spontaneously share food with others, even if they have the chance of consuming the food on their own.
source: Moreover, domesticated and wild rats have been shown to spontaneously share food with others, even if they have the chance of consuming the food on their own (Barnett, 1963; Colin and Desor, 1986; Grasmuck and Desor, 2002; Krafft et al., 1994; Littman et al., 1954).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barnett, 1963; Colin and Desor, 1986; Grasmuck and Desor, 2002; Krafft et al., 1994; Littman et al., 1954.

claim: Food donations are fine-tuned to the partner's need to receive help.
source: Food donations are fine-tuned to the partner's need to receive help (Schneeberger et al., 2012), which may be communicated visually (Márquez et al., 2015), acoustically (Łopuch and Popik, 2011) or as a combination of several cues (Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schneeberger et al., 2012; Márquez et al., 2015; Łopuch and Popik, 2011; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018b.

claim: When rats share food, they reciprocate help, that is they base their decision to provide food on previously received donations and pay back quid pro quo.
source: When rats share food, they reciprocate help, that is they base their decision to provide food on previously received donations and pay back quid pro quo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the text.

claim: The rule 'I help you because someone helped me', that is generalised reciprocity, is followed by female, but not male wild-derived rats.
source: The rule 'I help you because someone helped me', that is generalised reciprocity, is followed by female, but not male wild-derived rats (Rutte and Taborsky, 2007; Schweinfurth et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rutte and Taborsky, 2007 and Schweinfurth et al., 2019.

claim: When interacting with the same partner repeatedly, rats use direct reciprocity, that is 'I help you because you helped me'.
source: In addition, when interacting with the same partner repeatedly, rats use direct reciprocity, that is 'I help you because you helped me' (domesticated rats [Li and Wood, 2017; Simones, 2007; Viana et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2016], wild-derived rats [Dolivo and Taborsky, 2015a; Rutte and Taborsky, 2008; Schweinfurth et al., 2019; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2016; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2017; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018c; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018a; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018c; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2020]).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on domesticated and wild-derived rats.

claim: Rats not only take into account whether the partner has helped them in the past, but also the quality of received help and the eagerness of the partner to provide help.
source: Thereby, they not only take into account whether the partner has helped them in the past, but also the quality of received help (Dolivo and Taborsky, 2015b) and the eagerness of the partner to provide help (Schneeberger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dolivo and Taborsky, 2015b and Schneeberger et al., 2012.

claim: Wild-derived rats also exchange natural occurring allogrooming reciprocally.
source: Two recent studies showed that wild-derived rats also exchange natural occurring allogrooming reciprocally (Schweinfurth et al., 2017b; Stieger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schweinfurth et al., 2017b and Stieger et al., 2017.

claim: Rats that allogroom partners reciprocally live longer and develop fewer mammary tumours.
source: While allogrooming is a rather short affiliative behaviour, the reciprocal exchange has important life-long consequences, as rats that allogroom partners reciprocally live longer and develop fewer mammary tumours (Yee et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yee et al., 2008.

claim: Rats exchange food in an artificial setting against allogrooming as a natural behaviour.
source: Further, rats exchange food in an artificial setting against allogrooming as a natural behaviour (Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018c.

claim: Rats use information about toxic diets and hunting techniques from conspecifics, even if it conflicts with their personal information.
source: Rats do not only benefit from conspecifics of which they receive help, but they also gain important information from others, for example about toxic diets (Steininger, 1950) or hunting techniques (Galef, 1982). They use this information even if it conflicts with their personal information (Galef and Whiskin, 2008; Galef and Whiskin, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Steininger, 1950; Galef, 1982; Galef and Whiskin, 2008; Galef and Whiskin, 2000.

claim: When learning from others where to eat, wild and domesticated rats employ various methods including local enhancement, urine markings, learning from maternal milk, and copying preferences of other rats.
source: When learning from others where to eat, wild and domesticated rats employ various methods (reviewed in Galef and Laland, 2005). First, they show local enhancement, that is visiting food locations where other rats were observed (Galef, 1971). Second, locations can be communicated by urine markings, which are used by others to locate suitable feeding sides (Galef and Heiber, 1976). Third, already before eating solid food, domesticated rats learn from their mother which food is palatable due to diet cues in the maternal milk (Galef and Sherry, 1973). Finally, domesticated adult rats can learn to copy preferences of other rats (Galef and Wigmore, 1983), which can be based on the breath of conspecifics (Galef et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galef and Laland, 2005; Galef, 1971; Galef and Heiber, 1976; Galef and Sherry, 1973; Galef and Wigmore, 1983; Galef et al., 1988.

claim: The so acquired preferences, learned over few encounters only, can last for at least one month.
source: The so acquired preferences, learned over few encounters only, can last for at least one month (Galef and Whiskin, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galef and Whiskin, 2003.

claim: Wild rats show local differences in their hunting techniques that appear to fulfil the definition of culture.
source: Indeed, wild rats show local differences in their hunting techniques that appear to fulfil the definition of culture. These local hunting traditions include raiding bird nests (Austin, 1948), hunting for birds up to the size of ducks (Steininger, 1950), fishing for small fish (Coleman et al., 1948) and diving to collect mussels (Gandolfi and Parisi, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Austin, 1948; Steininger, 1950; Coleman et al., 1948; Gandolfi and Parisi, 1973.

claim: Rats observe others to infer information indirectly through transitive inference.
source: They also observe others to infer information indirectly through transitive inference (Vasconcelos, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vasconcelos, 2008.

claim: Domesticated rats can logically infer about hierarchical relations in artificial tests.
source: Domesticated rats can logically infer about hierarchical relations in artificial tests (Dusek and Eichenbaum, 1997; Roberts and Phelps, 1994): but see also Guez and Audley (2013), highlighting their socio-cognitive abilities.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dusek and Eichenbaum, 1997; Roberts and Phelps, 1994; Guez and Audley, 2013.

claim: Rats are known to use visual, acoustic and olfactory cues for communication.
source: Rats are known to use visual, acoustic and olfactory cues for communication (Whishaw and Kolb, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whishaw and Kolb, 2004.

claim: As rats are active mainly at dusk and dawn, their visual system is poorly developed compared to diurnal mammals.
source: As rats are active mainly at dusk and dawn (Telle, 1966), their visual system is poorly developed compared to diurnal mammals (Prusky et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Telle, 1966 and Prusky et al., 2002.

claim: Three main ultrasonic calls have been described in domesticated rats: an alarm call (frequency: 22 kHz, length: 300–3,000 ms), a social call (50 kHz, 20–80 ms) and an isolation call (40 kHz, 80–140 ms).
source: Three main ultrasonic calls have been described in domesticated rats (Brudzynski, 2009): an alarm call (frequency: 22 kHz, length: 300–3,000 ms), a social call (50 kHz, 20–80 ms) and an isolation call (40 kHz, 80–140 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brudzynski, 2009.

claim: Isolation calls are produced only by juvenile rats when they are separated from their litter or mother.
source: While the former two types are emitted by adults and juveniles alike and occur in a variety of contexts, the latter are produced only by juvenile rats when they are separated from their litter or mother (Hofer, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hofer, 1996.

claim: Social calls commonly are produced in a socio-positive context, that is during social play, joint exploration, cooperation and during copulations.
source: Social calls commonly are produced in a socio-positive context, that is during social play (Knutson et al., 1998), joint exploration (Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002), cooperation (Łopuch and Popik, 2011; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018b) and during copulations (Barfield et al., 1979), as they may lead to approach behaviours by others (Wöhr and Schwarting, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knutson et al., 1998; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002; Łopuch and Popik, 2011; Schweinfurth and Taborsky, 2018b; Barfield et al., 1979; Wöhr and Schwarting, 2007.

claim: Alarm calls are usually associated with socio-negative contexts, that is when being threatened by predators, being exposed to fearful situations, showing submissive displays, but also during copulations.
source: In contrast, alarm calls are usually associated with socio-negative contexts, that is when being threatened by predators (Blanchard et al., 1991), being exposed to fearful situations (Borta et al., 2006), showing submissive displays (Takahashi et al., 1983), but also during copulations (Barfield et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blanchard et al., 1991; Borta et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 1983; Barfield et al., 1979.

claim: Pitches of alarm calls differ across contexts, suggesting context specific modulations.
source: Although fluctuation around 22 kHz, pitches of alarm calls differ across contexts, suggesting context specific modulations (Brudzynski, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brudzynski, 2005.

claim: Domesticated rats actively scent mark objects or surfaces using urine or faeces by pressing their anogenital area or rubbing their flanks over the respective surface, possibly to signal dominance.
source: First, domesticated rats actively scent mark objects or surfaces using urine or faeces by pressing their anogenital area or rubbing their flanks over the respective surface, possibly to signal dominance (Grant and Mackintosh, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grant and Mackintosh, 1963.

claim: In wild rats, both sexes leave such marks probably for the same reasons.
source: In wild rats, both sexes leave such marks probably for the same reasons (Telle, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Telle, 1966.

claim: Rats mark the paths outside their burrow to optimise foraging efficiency and to increase protection from predators by using them as escape paths.
source: Furthermore, they mark the paths outside their burrow (Galef and Buckley, 1996) to optimise foraging efficiency and to increase protection from predators by using them as escape paths (Calhoun, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galef and Buckley, 1996 and Calhoun, 1962.

claim: Rats possess glands across their body, whose odours transfer information of relatedness and individual identity.
source: Rats also possess glands across their body, whose odours transfer information of relatedness (Hepper, 1987a) and individual identity (Gheusi et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hepper, 1987a and Gheusi et al., 1997.

claim: Controlling large rat populations has been mainly ineffective, especially in urban areas.
source: Despite huge effort, controlling large rat populations has been mainly ineffective, especially in urban areas (Duron et al., 2017; Himsworth et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duron et al., 2017 and Himsworth et al., 2013a.

claim: It took a team of several researchers 18 weeks to capture a single individual rat on a small island, although this animal was equipped with a radio collar.
source: Trapping rats is notoriously difficult, exemplified by the fact that it took a team of several researchers 18 weeks to capture a single individual on a small island, although this animal was equipped with a radio collar (Russell et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell et al., 2005.

claim: In 7% to 14% of all cases, traps do not kill the rats but injure them, causing ethical issues.
source: In 7% to 14% of all cases, traps do not kill the rats but injure them, causing ethical issues (Meerburg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meerburg et al., 2008.

claim: The social life of urban rats, although causing the most problems, is the least understood.
source: It should be noted that especially the social life of urban rats, although causing the most problems, is the least understood (Desvars-Larrive et al., 2018; Parsons et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Desvars-Larrive et al., 2018 and Parsons et al., 2017.

claim: Rats prefer spending time with a conspecific over receiving heroin or methamphetamine, even if they are addicted to these substances.
source: Their great social need is highlighted by the fact that rats prefer spending time with a conspecific over receiving heroin or methamphetamine, even if they are addicted to these substances (Venniro et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venniro et al., 2018.

claim: Rats put more effort in joining familiar conspecifics than inanimate objects or larger cages.
source: They also put more effort in joining familiar conspecifics than inanimate objects or larger cages (Patterson-Kane et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Patterson-Kane et al., 2002.

claim: Isolated rats showed marked differences in their behaviour, cognition, physiology and neurobiology that is likely to impact the translatability of results obtained on such animals.
source: Finally, isolated rats showed marked differences in their behaviour, cognition, physiology and neurobiology that is likely to impact the translatability of results obtained on such animals (Arakawa, 2018; Mumtaz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arakawa, 2018 and Mumtaz et al., 2018.

claim: Peer rejection during adolescence has been shown to have long-lasting effects in the brain and social behaviour of rats.
source: For instance, peer rejection during adolescence has been shown to have long-lasting effects in the brain and social behaviour of rats (Schneider et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schneider et al., 2016.

claim: Rats that interact with a familiar partner in pain show afterwards stronger pain reaction themselves compared to rats that interact with an unfamiliar partner in pain.
source: For example, rats that interact with a familiar partner in pain show afterwards stronger pain reaction themselves compared to rats that interact with an unfamiliar partner in pain (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Rats have been shown to possess mirror neurons that are active when experiencing pain and when observing a conspecific in pain.
source: Rats have been shown to possess mirror neurons that are active when experiencing pain and when observing a conspecific in pain (Carrillo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carrillo et al., 2019.

claim: The presence of a partner can have buffering effects as rats seem to be less stressed when exposed to a stressor when in company of a cage mate.
source: At the same time the presence of a partner can have buffering effects as rats seem to be less stressed when exposed to a stressor when in company of a cage mate (Kiyokawa et al., 2004) or when they can interact with a social partner shortly after a stressful event (Akyazi and Eraslan, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kiyokawa et al., 2004 and Akyazi and Eraslan, 2014.

claim: Experiencing stressful situations together with a cage mate leads to a lack of fear conditioning towards such stressors.
source: In line with this finding, experiencing stressful situations together with a cage mate leads to a lack of fear conditioning towards such stressors (Kiyokawa et al., 2007), which might be important for experiments that are based on repeated treatments.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kiyokawa et al., 2007.

claim: Chronically stressed laboratory animals are more likely to become aggressive, as well as physically and mentally sick.
source: Chronically stressed laboratory animals are more likely to become aggressive, as well as physically and mentally sick (de Boer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Boer et al., 2017.

claim: Several million rats were killed in the 90s every year in the UK alone.
source: Exact data on the number of killed rats is not available, besides an estimation of several million rats that were killed in the 90 s every year in the UK alone (reviewed in Mason and Littin, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mason and Littin, 2003.

claim: Poisoning with anticoagulants causes long-lasting discomfort and pain in poisoned and conscious individuals over an average period of 7.2 days.
source: However, it is also the least humane way because it interferes with the rat's ability to forage or escape predators, leaves sub-lethally poisoned individuals ill, affects non-target species (including children) and causes long-lasting discomfort and pain in poisoned and conscious individuals over an average period of 7.2 days (Mason and Littin, 2003; Meerburg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mason and Littin, 2003 and Meerburg et al., 2008.
